newsitem.title: JAPAN: Weak petrol prices to hit Japan refiners' profits.
newsitem.headline: Weak petrol prices to hit Japan refiners' profits.

text.p: Sliding retail gasoline prices are expected to continue pressuring profits at Japan's oil companies, despite their forecasts of better results for fiscal year 1997/98, analysts said on Wednesday.

"Gasoline prices at the pump are falling all over Japan," said Toshinori Itoh, senior analyst for Daiwa Institute of Research Ltd. "It would be quite difficult for oil firms to cover profits lost from gasoline sales with cost-cutting efforts."

The average retail price for gasoline fell one yen to 106 yen per litre in late April and slipped further to 105 yen a litre as of May 26, amid intense competition among petrol stations, according to a weekly survey by the Oil Information Service Centre.
A dip of one yen per litre in retail gasoline prices shaves about 53 billion yen from annual profits for the domestic oil industry, Itoh said.

The major Japanese oil firms last week and earlier this week announced declines in current profits for fiscal 1996/97, ended in March, mainly because of a lag in passing higher crude oil prices on to wholesale prices for domestic oil products.
It usually takes a month or two for Japanese oil firms to adjust their oil product prices to reflect fluctuations in crude oil import costs.
Almost all of Japan's oil companies said, however, that their current profits for the business year ending next March will improve as a result of rigorous cost-cutting.
Idemitsu Kosan Co Ltd said its current profits would reach about 10 billion yen for fiscal 1997/98, up from the previous year's 7.6 billion yen.
The refiner said it carried out a 12 billion yen cost-cutting programme in fiscal 1996/97 and intends to slash costs further in such fields as oil refining and domestic distribution.
Other major refiners, including Nippon Oil Co Ltd, Japan Energy Corp, Mitsubishi Oil Co Ltd and Cosmo Oil Co Ltd, plan to carry out similar streamlining operations in the current business year.
Analysts also said falling gasoline prices will affect the financial results of oil firms differently, depending on how rigorously they have streamlined operations.
"Unlike the old days, there are not going to be similar financial results for every firm," said an analyst with Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics Inc.
"Only those firms which are in an advanced stage of streamlining can increase profits despite falling gasoline prices," he said.
